problem: Long-range outdoor navigation and object search is hampered by the short reliable depth/LiDAR horizon (~10 m). Geometry-only frontier exploration is myopic, memoryless vision-only methods (LRN) oscillate and get stuck in dead-ends, and open-vocabulary mapping cannot localize targets beyond depth range.
motivation: Field robots (search-and-rescue, inspection) must find language-specified targets hundreds of metres away without maps or GNSS. Images carry cues beyond the depth horizon (openings, trail ends, terrain type, the target itself), while a sparse graph gives scalable memory and geometric safety. Combining them should give efficient and robust exploration.
key_idea: Score the geometric frontier nodes of a sparse navigation graph using a foundation-model vision module (ExploRFM: traversability, visual frontiers, open-vocabulary similarity), and localize far targets with a particle-based multi-view triangulation.
insight: Vision cues beyond the depth range decide which frontier to pursue, while graph memory lets the robot backtrack from dead-ends. In the dead-end experiment WildOS succeeded in all runs while memoryless LRN needed human intervention each time. In the fence experiment vision-guided scoring picked the corridor opening instead of the blocked direct path, and adding traversability to frontier scoring avoids unreachable frontiers that LRN pursues. Frozen RADIO features with a head trained on only 350 annotated frontier images generalize across terrains.
method: Navigation graph: sparse graph built incrementally from the local LiDAR traversability map; nodes store free and explored radii from SDFs; nodes next to unknown space are frontier nodes; collision-free edges connect neighbours.

ExploRFM: frozen C-RADIO-V3-B (90M) with NACLIP and SigLIP adaptor for language-aligned features; cosine similarity with a SigLIP-2 text query gives an object mask; two deconv heads predict visual traversability (trained on RUGD) and visual frontiers (350 manually annotated GrandTour images, weighted BCE).

Goal triangulation: for each view with a detected mask, sample 1000 particles along pixel rays at 1-100 m depth; weight each particle by the sum of 1/(distance to mask-centroid rays over views); weighted mean gives a coarse 3D goal beyond depth range.

Cross-modal frontier scoring: project each frontier node into the 3 camera images and score it as max over pixels of G_conf (goal heading) x R_conf (min-cost image path over traversable pixels) x F_conf (frontier confidence); goal-agnostic with 16 heading bins; scores are cached and updated only when the robot is closer.

Hierarchical planner: an auxiliary goal node is connected to each frontier with cost z(s)*d~, where z = 1 - alpha*log(s+eps) and d~ is a safe distance from a coarse explored-occupancy grid; Dijkstra picks the path; a local goal 5 m ahead goes to Nav2.
System: Spot quadruped with Ouster LiDAR, 3 RealSense cameras, DLIO odometry, Elevation Mapping CuPy; everything onboard on a Jetson AGX Orin (ExploRFM at 1.4 Hz).

setting.backbone: C-RADIO-V3-B (frozen) + two small deconv heads (trained), SigLIP-2 text encoder; hand-designed graph planner
setting.training_data: Traversability head: RUGD (7436 images, 24 classes); frontier head: 350 manually annotated GrandTour images; language alignment pretrained by RADIO
setting.observation: 3 RGB cameras (left/front/right) + Ouster LiDAR + IMU, LiDAR-inertial odometry pose, no GNSS
setting.action_space: high-level graph path to a 5 m local waypoint, executed by Nav2 as continuous velocity commands
setting.privileged: an approximate prior goal location/heading g0 given by the operator at mission start; no GT map

numbers_note: No numeric tables. The fence experiment (3 runs, distance/time mean ± 95% CI) is reported only in Fig. 4(c), and the dead-end and urban experiments are qualitative, so no exact values are in the text.
results: On Spot in the field, WildOS completed a ~150 m open-vocabulary search for the 'NASA logo' and zero-shot searches for orange flag, garbage container and golf cart. Against LRN and Vanilla GraphNav it gave shorter distance/time with smaller variance in the fence test. It succeeded in 3/3 dead-end runs while LRN needed human intervention every time. It also worked in urban scenes without retraining.
limitations: Oscillation between distant high-scoring frontiers in large areas; explored regions are approximated as circles, which can create spurious frontiers.
No visual feature memory at graph nodes, so retrospective query search is impossible; a single similarity threshold is used for all object categories.
Evaluation is small-scale and qualitative (3 runs per scenario, few scenes, only two baselines, no success-rate benchmark); needs an approximate prior goal.
